questions.q: Your friends all play Minecraft on their phones and an Xbox. Which edition of server should you set up on the Pi?
choices: Java Edition, because it is the original and most compatible version.
Bedrock Edition, because that is what phones, tablets, and consoles run.
Either one — Bedrock and Java players can join the same server.
Neither — consoles cannot connect to a Raspberry Pi server.
questions.explain: Phones, tablets, Xbox, PlayStation, Switch, and the Windows 10/11 app all run Bedrock Edition, so you need a Bedrock server. Java and Bedrock players cannot join the same ordinary server, so the edition must match the devices your group actually uses.

questions.q: On a Pi 5 with 8 GB of RAM, why should you NOT set the Java server's memory to -Xmx8G?
choices: Minecraft refuses to start with more than 4 GB of memory.
The operating system needs its own share of RAM, so allocating all of it will cause the server to freeze or crash.
Higher memory settings always make the server slower.
The Pi can only address 4 GB of RAM at a time.
questions.explain: The -Xmx value is the maximum memory the Java server may use, but the Pi's operating system also needs RAM to run. If you hand the whole 8 GB to Minecraft, nothing is left for the system and the Pi will run out of memory and crash. Leaving 3–4 GB free is the safe rule — so -Xmx6G is sensible on an 8 GB board.

questions.q: Why do you run the Java (Paper) server once, then edit eula.txt, before it will actually start your world?
choices: The first run downloads the rest of the server files from the internet.
Editing eula.txt sets the server's memory limit.
Minecraft requires you to accept its End-User Licence Agreement; the first run creates eula.txt and stops until you change eula=false to eula=true.
The first run tests whether your Pi has enough RAM to continue.
questions.explain: Mojang requires you to agree to the End-User Licence Agreement before any server will run. The first launch generates eula.txt set to false and then exits. You change the line to eula=true to record your acceptance, and the next launch generates the world and starts the server.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of registering your Minecraft server as a systemd service?
choices: It makes the server use less RAM than running it by hand.
It automatically starts the server when the Pi boots and restarts it if it crashes, with no one logged in.
It lets Bedrock and Java players connect to the same world.
It encrypts the connection so the server is safe to expose to the internet.
questions.explain: Run by hand, the server only lives as long as your Terminal window is open. A systemd service is supervised by Linux: it launches the server on boot, keeps it running in the background whether or not anyone is logged in, and (with Restart=on-failure) relaunches it after a crash — exactly what an always-on server needs.

questions.q: You want friends from their own homes to join, and you want the safest, simplest method. What should you reach for first?
choices: Put the Pi directly on the internet with no firewall so connections are fastest.
Use a tunnel service such as playit.gg, which gives the server a public address without opening ports on your router or exposing your home IP.
Email each friend a copy of the world folder to play separately.
Forward every port on your router to the Pi to be safe.
questions.explain: A tunnel service like playit.gg connects outward from the Pi and hands your friends a public address, without opening any ports on your router or revealing your home IP — avoiding the riskiest part of self-hosting. Traditional port forwarding also works but exposes your Pi to the internet, so you should secure it (and read the security chapter) first. Forwarding every port is never a good idea.
